item.title: Yemeni government launches offensive to seize all areas from Iran-backed Houthis
item.description:
YEMEN-SAUDI-ISRAN-US-ISRAEL-WAR

Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government said on Sunday it was launching a major military campaign to recapture all areas of the country controlled by the Iran-backed Houthis.

The government’s armed forces would press the offensive “until the country is liberated from the grip of the terrorist militia,” Yemeni President Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address. A military spokesman later called on the Houthis to lay down their weapons.

The Houthis, known formally as Ansar Allah, have held Yemen’s capital Sanaa and vast parts of the northwest, where most of the population live, since 2014. They have so far withstood a series of attacks over the years by Saudi Arabia, the UAE and their Western allies, and have updated their weaponry with the help of Iran.

The movement launched a surprise offensive last month which captured the strategic Bab el-Mandeb strait and some 150 km (90 miles) of coast on the Red Sea in a matter of weeks, giving the Houthis new leverage over the international shipping route.

That advance also opened a new front in the wider US-Israeli war launched in February against Iran, to which Tehran’s responses included choking oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, to the other side of the Arabian Peninsula.

Bangladesh condemns Houthi drone attack on Madinah infrastructure

Houthis say they struck Saudi Arabia

As the Yemeni government, known as the Presidential Leadership Council, made its announcement, the Houthis said they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco sites in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia.

They claimed the attacks caused major fires and were in response to what they said were 50 Saudi-led air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours.

There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.

Alimi said the decision to launch the counteroffensive came after all chances of de-escalating the conflict had been exhausted.

He thanked Saudi Arabia for its support and called on Yemen's regional allies and international partners to support PLC forces and institutions.

Regional and western officials had told Reuters earlier this week that Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies were planning to launch an assault on the Houthis, with the Saudis leading aerial combat and Yemeni forces fighting on the ground.

Houthis say struck oil facility near Riyadh, as Saudis hit Sanaa

New front in Mideast war

The US is already providing intelligence to support Riyadh's operations in Yemen, while some regional and European nations are providing mainly defensive military aid to the kingdom, six people with knowledge of the Saudi preparations told Reuters.

The United States’ war on Iran has decimated a layer of Iranian military and political leadership, but has also entangled Washington in a new engagement in the Middle East and depleted crucial military hardware.

Yemen has been mired in conflict for years, with an array of local armed groups and factions backed by competing regional and international actors.

After a popular uprising that was part of the Arab Spring movements in 2011, the Houthis, an armed group of Zaidi Shi’ite Muslims, captured Sanaa.

The Saudi-backed PLC, which is also recognised by the United Nations, has since the Houthi takeover controlled the south and east of the country, based in the former South Yemen capital of Aden.

Saudi Arabia entered Yemen's civil war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition in support of the PLC, but failed to defeat the Houthis.

A truce agreed between the warring parties in 2022 largely held until this year, when the Houthis launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi shipping and oil infrastructure in a spillover from the Iran war.

Saudi plans Houthi offensive with 100,000 Yemeni troops, US, other countries' support

Houthis on front foot

The Houthis have maintained the initiative on the ground since seizing control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in their lightning offensive last month that saw government forces collapse.

Bab el-Mandeb is the southern exit passage of the Red Sea, a key shipping route between the Mediterranean and Asia that has assumed even more importance this year as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.

In the last 48 hours, the Houthis have also made gains against government and local forces on strategic hilltops near Yemen's Taiz, military sources said, advancing on the last road between the city and Aden on the southern coast.

Houthi control over the Taiz-Aden road would lead to an effective siege of the city, Yemen's third-largest, inhabited by hundreds of thousands of civilians and where thousands of government forces are also stationed.

The city is important not just for its strategic location; Alimi is from the region, and a siege of Taiz would amplify an already-dire humanitarian situation in the country.

Three in four ​families in parts of Yemen are going hungry from the impact of the surge in fighting, ‌which has displaced tens of thousands of people and disrupted supplies to millions, the World Food Programme said last week.

item.title: House rents rise 27pc in 4 years, taking a bigger bite out of incomes
item.description:
Shahadat Hossain works for a private company in the capital. He earns a total of Tk 39,000 a month. Until recently, he lived in a shared rented accommodation. He recently got married and now needs a small flat, preferably close to his office in Mohammadpur.

Over the past week, he has searched extensively for a two-room flat in Adabor, Shekhertek and areas around the Mohammadpur bus stand. But the rents are beyond his means, with nothing available for less than Tk 18,000.

If he rents a flat at this rate, gas and electricity bills will be added to the rent, along with a service charge. Altogether, the monthly cost would exceed Tk 20,000.

Speaking to Prothom Alo on Sunday, Shahadat Hossain said, “If half my salary goes towards housing, how am I supposed to manage in this high-cost market?”

Prime Minister inaugurates World Habitat Day 2026
Shahadat HossainIf half my salary goes towards housing, how am I supposed to manage in this high-cost market?

Expressing his helplessness, he said he had been forced to decide to look for cheaper accommodation much farther from his office. Although this would make commuting more difficult, he said it would save some money to cover other expenses.

Like Shahadat, almost all people in Dhaka on limited and fixed incomes face a similar situation. A large portion of their income has to be spent on housing. Even then, they cannot always find a home that meets their needs. Moreover, once a house is rented, most landlords increase the rent almost every year.

According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), house rents in the country have increased by around 27 per cent over the past four years. In reality, however, rents are rising at a faster rate than the government’s figures suggest. The increase has been particularly sharp in Dhaka.

Four years ago, Fozayel Ahmed rented a three-room flat in East Goran for Tk 20,000. He said the rent has now risen to Tk 27,000. It has been increased three times, meaning a 35 per cent rise.

Four years ago, Fozayel Ahmed rented a three-room flat in East Goran for Tk 20,000. He said the rent has now risen to Tk 27,000. It has been increased three times, meaning a 35 per cent rise. Electricity and gas bills have also increased during this period. He has had to cut back on other expenses to cover the additional costs.

The United Nations Economic and Social Council’s World Urbanization Prospects 2025 report says around 36.6 million people now live in Dhaka city and its surrounding areas. Dhaka is the world’s second-most populous city.

A large proportion of this vast population lives in rented accommodation. The government enacted the House Rent Control Act in 1991, but the law has remained largely ineffective. This is because regulations needed to enforce the law have still not been formulated. It is against this backdrop that World Habitat Day is being observed today, Monday.

AHM Shafiquzzaman, president, CABRents are high in Dhaka because demand for housing exceeds supply. In many cases, landlords also have legitimate reasons for raising rents. However, there is no mechanism to monitor whether the increase is reasonable or whether excessive costs are being imposed on tenants.

Consumer Association of Bangladesh (CAB) President AHM Shafiquzzaman told Prothom Alo that rents are high in Dhaka because demand for housing exceeds supply. In many cases, landlords also have legitimate reasons for raising rents.

However, he said there is no mechanism to monitor whether the increase is reasonable or whether excessive costs are being imposed on tenants. For this, it is essential to formulate regulations under the House Rent Control Act. This would make it possible to resolve rent-related disputes within a legal framework.

Additional house rent: Law on paper, not in reality

How much have rents increased?

Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) publishes a house rent index every three months. According to the government agency, house rents in Bangladesh increased by around 27 per cent between July 2022 and the end of July 2026.

This is the national average. Rents have increased even more depending on demand and location. In Dhaka, for example, both the ammount of rents and the rate of increase are the highest.

item.title: Two Indian nationals shot in BSF firing at Kurigram border
item.description:
Two Indian nationals were seriously injured after the Indian Border Security Force (BSF) allegedly opened fire on them along the Daikhawa border in Ulipur upazila of Kurigram on Sunday afternoon.
The injured men were identified as Ismail Hossain, 35, and Khaja Abdul Alim, 39, residents of Barobalu village under Sukchar Police Station in Assam’s South Salmara-Mankachar district.
After being shot, they crossed into Bangladesh and were rescued by local residents, who took them to a clinic in Rangpur. Later, the Detective Branch (DB) of Rangpur Metropolitan Police transferred them to Rangpur Medical College Hospital for better treatment.
Rangpur Metropolitan Police Deputy Commissioner and DB chief Sanatan Chakraborty confirmed the matter to Dhaka Tribune, saying the two men were arrested in a case filed over illegal entry into Bangladesh.
Doctors found multiple pellet wounds on their bodies, while one of them also sustained a burn-like injury.
The circumstances surrounding their presence in the border area remain unclear. DB officials are investigating the incident, including why the BSF allegedly opened fire on the two Indian nationals.
Local residents suspect the men had crossed into the border area to smuggle cattle and were shot by the BSF after being mistaken for Bangladeshi cattle smugglers.
The injured men, however, claimed they had gone to a char area near the border to graze cattle. They alleged that BSF personnel detained them and tried to push them into Bangladesh.
According to the men, they resisted, leading to a scuffle, after which the BSF allegedly opened fire and left them injured on the Bangladesh side.
Khaja Abdul Alim, one of the injured men, said they were Indian citizens and had gone to the char to graze cattle. He alleged that BSF personnel accused them of being Bangladeshi cattle smugglers and took them to a char area, where an argument broke out before they were shot.
He appealed to the governments of Bangladesh and India to facilitate their return home.
Police and local residents said the BSF personnel fired at Ismail and Khaja from an area near Assam’s Narayanpur land port towards Daikhawar Char in the Brahmaputra River area of Ulipur.

item.title: US-German trio wins Nobel Prize in Medicine for work on optogenetics
item.description:
The Nobel medicine prize was awarded Monday to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their pioneering work in the field of optogenetics.
Optogenetics involves controlling nerve signals with light, and helps researchers understand how specific cell types contribute to behaviors like learning, fear, addiction and movement.
The trio were honored “for their discovery of a molecular switch for nerve cells,” the Nobel Assembly said.
Using light, researchers are now able to switch individual neural circuits on or off in a brain.
They have been able to reveal neural circuits governing specific memories, feelings, and behaviors relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders.
In clinical medicine, the method is being used in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairment, and may one day lead to treatments for disorders such as Parkinson’s disease and epilepsy.
“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel committee, said in a statement.
“Optogenetics has fundamentally altered our understanding of the brain. Every day brings new discoveries, helping to solve one of humanity’s great mysteries: how our incredible brain works,” the Nobel Assembly said.
The secretary general of the assembly, Thomas Perlmann, told reporters he was able to reach the three laureates by phone to break the news.
“That was great to talk to them. I first called Deisseroth he was very tired when he answered. He was definitely asleep, but he woke up,” he said.
In the early 2000s, Hegemann and Nagel were examining why a single-celled alga was able to swim toward a light source.
They discovered an algal protein with unique properties, called channelrhodopsin, found on the surface of the cell.
When illuminated by blue light, a channel opens through the protein.
Charged ions then flow into the cell, creating an electrical impulse. They found that any cell they put the protein in became light sensitive.
Deisseroth then introduced the gene for channelrhodopsin into nerve cells from rats.
By illuminating the cells with blue light, he was able to trigger a nerve signal.
He published his breakthrough in 2005, and two years later, made the light-controlled switch for nerve cells work in the brains of living mice.
In 2021, Deisseroth and Hegemann won the Lasker Prize for their work in the field, often considered a precursor to the Nobel.
Deisseroth, 54, is a professor at Stanford University in the US, while Hegemann, 71, is a neuroscience professor at Humboldt University of Berlin.
Nagel, 73, is a biophysics professor at the University of Wurzburg.
The Nobel prize for physics will be announced on Tuesday, followed by the chemistry prize on Wednesday and the literature prize on Thursday.
Some pundits have suggested that for literature, the Swedish Academy could follow up last year’s award to Hungary’s Laszlo Krasznahorkai with a woman writer, possibly from Central or Latin America.
Argentine author Samanta Schweblin, 48, could be one such pick, literary critic Lina Kalmteg told AFP.
Perhaps the most keenly anticipated award is that due on Friday, the peace prize -- the only Nobel to be awarded in Oslo.
This year, some experts have suggested the jury could choose a laureate who enjoys broad consensus, after last year’s winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, stirred controversy.
Among possible laureates this year are a joint prize to Save the Children and Mykola Kuleba, a Ukrainian children’s rights activist campaigning for the return of Ukrainian children illegally taken to Russia from occupied territories.
Others include Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms (ERR), a vast network of volunteers risking their lives to help people facing the double threat of war and hunger, and the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) after the deadliest year on record for the profession in 2025.
The economics prize wraps up the Nobel season on October 12.
This year’s laureates will receive their prizes -- a diploma, a gold medal and a $1.2-million cheque -- on December 10, the anniversary of the death in 1896 of the prize’s creator, scientist Alfred Nobel.

item.title: Russia ‘pneumonic plague’: What we know about the quarantine in Siberia after a researcher’s death
item.description:
U.S. investigators are closely monitoring reports that dozens of people are in quarantine after the death of a Russian laboratory worker studying the plague in Siberia.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the State Department, the Administration for Strategic Preparedness and Response, and other U.S. government agencies are trying to determine what happened after a 28-year-old female lab technician at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia died after being diagnosed with a pneumonia of “unknown” origin, per Russia’s infection disease agency Rospotrebnadzor, as reported by CNN.

On Monday, secretary of state Marco Rubio told reporters that Russian officials said other workers could be affected.

“We’re watching and monitoring it closely,” Rubio said. “I don’t think it’s cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on it.”

The lab technician’s cause of death remains unclear. One Russian news outlet reported that she “allegedly broke a test tube containing the pneumonic plague pathogen” on Friday, September 25, and died at a hospital soon after.

In the meantime, nearly 200 people who may have come in contact with the researcher are now under medical observation, NBC News reported.

Rospotrebnadzor announced the mayor of Shelekhov, the town at the epicenter of the potential outbreak, has enacted a “comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures,” The Washington Post reported. The district is located in far eastern Siberia, near the Mongolian border.

“Plague is a potentially life-threatening disease caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, spread to people through bites from infected rodent fleas or, less often, direct contact with an infected animal, according to the CDC. “It can be cured with antibiotics, but treatment must be given quickly,” the CDC adds.

The most common forms of plague are bubonic, pneumonic, and septicemic. The “Black Death,” as it was known, is a pandemic said to be caused by the plague, which swept across Europe in the 14th century, killing tens of millions of people.

Pneumonic plague develops when bacteria spread to the lungs of a patient with untreated bubonic or septicemic plague. It’s the most serious form of the disease and is the only form of plague that can be spread between people, with an incubation period as short as one day, per the CDC.

Hegseth’s Vision for a New American Military
item.description:
“It's worth saying again so that the fake news understands it. We are no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that: No fanny, no fatties, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals, just warriors -- just tough, ready, committed troops. The War Department, as you know, is colorblind, gender neutral, and merit-based. Or, as the President likes to say to me: ‘Pete, central casting. I want central casting.’”

That was Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth speaking on The State of the Force last Wednesday at the Marine Corps Base, Quantico, Virginia to a group of 600 selected O-3 junior officers (Captains in the Army, Marine Corps, Air Force, and Space Force; Lieutenants in the Navy and Coast Guard) and E-6 enlisted service personnel (Staff Sergeants in the Army and Marine Corps; Petty Officers First Class in the Navy and Coast Guard; Technical Sergeants in the Air Force and Space Force).

President Trump wants a military that looks like “central casting,” and Defense Secretary Hegseth, who looks and acts as if he, himself, came out of central casting, gave last week’s speech, reminiscent to anyone over 45 of the 1970 movie Patton, where George C. Scott playing Gen. George S. Patton also spoke before a full-screen American flag.

“The ideological clowns are out,” Hegseth said, “The patriotic cowboys are in with testosterone testing on top.”

He is correct.

He spoke of bringing back PT (physical training) “for every combat MOS (military occupational specialty),” adding, “We now have a combat field test, again, set at the highest male standard, only because combat doesn't care. That means two PT tests every year for every unit.”

As for picking senior leaders, Hegseth said, “We got rid of the DEI-based (diversity, equity and inclusion), social, emotional, evaluations known in the Army as BCAP [Battalion Commander Assessment Program] and CCAP [Colonels Command Assessment Program]. You won't have to endure them. They were [former-Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Mark A.] Milley and [former Defense Secretary Lloyd] Austin specials, intended to create politically-correct quotas for race and gender. Under the guise of double-blind psychology assessments, the previous administration forced out so-called toxic leaders in favor of promoting risk-averse, get-along to go-along conformists.”

However, Hegseth left out the important fact that BCAP and CCAP were products of the first Trump administration, put together by Casey Wardynski, then-President Trump’s appointed Assistant Secretary of the Army for Manpower and Reserve Affairs.

In prepared testimony for a March 11, 2020, Senate Armed Services Subcommittee on Personnel, Wardynski said, “The Army is currently prototyping, piloting, or implementing talent management initiatives from Talent Based Branching (TBB) to Battalion Commander

Assessment Program (BCAP), with the goal of implementing most of these initiatives by December 2020… Exit interviews and surveys from participants, board members, and distinguished visitors indicate BCAP is better than the legacy system for selecting battalion commanders and other key Lieutenant Colonel positions. Seven hundred and fifty candidates participated in the first iteration of the BCAP in January and February 2020.”

In a September 21, 2020, Army release about testing the new Colonels Command Assessment Program (CCAP) for bias at Fort Knox, Kentucky, Wardynski is quoted saying of the CCAP program, “When we started things like talent management and then this [CCAP], the question of fairness came up. A lot of the focus of fairness was to the individual.”

Although Milley was Army Chief of Staff at the time Wardynski’s BCAP and CCAP were being introduced, then Gen. Austin was head of Central Command and not involved.

Since January 25, 2025, when he became Defense Secretary, Hegseth has changed the senior leadership of the military and even has plans that could affect the leadership in years to come, and I will discuss that below.

First I want to point out that Wardynski was not the only originator that Hegseth ignored during last week’s speech.

For example, former-Defense Secretary Ash Carter and his Deputy Defense Secretary Robert Work in 2015 established the Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) which was the initial effort to bridge the gap between the Defense Department and commercial technology through rapid investments in autonomous systems, human-machine teaming, and even early Artificial Intelligence (AI).

Project Maven, linked to DIU in 2017, focused on integrating computer vision and AI into drone operations, allowing computer algorithms to autonomously scan hours of aerial drone video footage to detect and tag potential tactical targets.

This sounds a lot like Hegseth’s new Autonomous Warfare Command (AutoWarCom). And to tie the connection further to Carter and Work’s DIU, Hegseth named Owen West, who up-to-now has been DIU’s Director, to be Chief Executive Officer of AutoWarCom.

Then there is Project Meridian, which is supposed to -- in Hegseth’s words -- “Creatively look to the future and identify the domains that we must conquer and capabilities we must master.”

We old-timers knew Andrew (Andy) Marshall and his Office of Net Assessment at the Pentagon which was started in 1973. With a small staff and a wide range of consultants, Marshall covered many areas related to national security. When he retired in 2015, his work was carried on until Hegseth disestablished it in March 2025.

Hegseth’s March 2025 memo called for a plan to rebuild the Marshall office in a manner “consistent with [Hegseth’s] priorities.”

Project Meridian may be that. As Hegseth described it last week, “We need to be looking forward into the future to achieve technological and military dominance on the battlefield for

decades to come. It is futuristic on purpose. Their work will be focused on discovering, developing, and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes without any creative limitations or restrictions.”

Hegseth said last week that he has from the beginning wanted a 20 percent reduction of flag officers “across the board,” adding, “Now, the media calls that a purge. I call it accountability, long overdue and frankly the bare minimum…You see you can't change a culture with the same people who enabled it.”

A list of those fired, compiled by CBS, is impressive: Air Force General Charles Q. Brown, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff; Navy Admiral Lisa Franchetti, chief of naval operations; General James Slife, Air Force vice chief of staff; General Randy George, Army chief of staff; General David Allvin, Air Force chief of staff; Army Lieutenant General Joseph B. Berger III, Army Judge Advocate General; Air Force Lieutenant General Charles Plummer, Air Force Judge Advocate General of the Air Force; Admiral Alvin Holsey, head of U.S. Southern Command; General Christopher Donahue, head of U.S. Army Europe and Africa; Air Force General Timothy Haugh, NSA director and head of U.S. Cyber Command; Lieutenant General Jeffrey Kruse, head of the Defense Intelligence Agency; Air Force Lieutenant General Jennifer Short, senior military assistant to Defense Secretary; Vice Admiral Nancy Lacore, Navy Reserve chief; Rear Admiral Milton Sands, head of Naval Special Warfare Command; General David Hodne, Army Transformation and Training Command; and Major General William Green, head of the Army Chaplain Corps.

In addition, I add Navy Secretary John Phelan and Army Secretary Dan Driscoll.

Needless to say, nothing like this has happened in the past to the U.S. military, and it doesn’t end there. We don’t know the full extent of the individuals Hegseth has knocked off promotion lists, although indications are clear they are most often women and minorities.

In another effort to affect the future, Hegseth not only has sought to force changes in the Service Academies’ curricula and civilian tenured teaching staffs, he announced in last week’s speech an attempt to influence college ROTC units and thus the future generation of young officers.

He also announced establishment of a new program, America’s Core of Cadets, to be initiated at five specified institutions: Louisiana State University (LSU), Liberty University, Tuskegee University, Mississippi State University, and Hillsdale College.

The publication Inside Higher Ed reported last week that LSU will establish a four-year military or national security program; create a self-governed student military organization – a cadet corps -- led by an independent commandant who reports to LSU’s president; and cadet members will be required to wear uniforms during all academic hours.

On top of all this, Hegseth also announced establishment of an Office of Religious Affairs, which will report straight to the Defense Secretary, or as he put it: “No staff filters, no bureaucratic dilution, a direct line to the Secretary. This is not going to be a paper-pushing shop. It's going to have real teeth. They'll protect budgets, demand infrastructure, and strengthen religious support.”

To justify this religious office, Hegseth pointed out, “Less than five percent of our force identifies as non-religious. Less than five percent. Meaning 95 percent of our force recognizes an almighty God.”

As with other statements made by Hegseth, this is not totally true.

According to a 2019 study conducted by the Congressional Research Service, approximately 73 percent of all military service members identify as people of faith, compared to less than three percent who are atheist or agnostic. Religious diversity in the military is broadly representative of the U.S. population, with nearly 70 percent of active duty military personnel who consider themselves to be Christian.

Hegseth said last week, “Our department is, you might say, putting on the full armor of God, because while we wage physical war, we all know the real battle is spiritual.”

Reviewing all Hegseth is doing, as a drafted, two-year Army veteran from the 1950s, I would say our Defense Secretary is taking the spirit of true government service out of the military I have known.

item.title: CM Afridi slams Governor Kundi for 'unconstitutional' meetings, claims move intended to provoke KP govt
item.description:
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi on Wednesday slammed Governor Faisal Karim Kundi for holding “unconstitutional” meetings, contending that the move was an “attack on democracy”.

His remarks came a day after Governor Kundi chaired a meeting with the KP chief secretary and inspector general (IG) on the province’s security situation.

Addressing the 60th cabinet meeting in Peshawar, Afridi said that the KP governor, who belonged to the PPP, staged a “drama” yesterday by summoning the meeting and termed the move “unconstitutional”.

“The governor convening such a meeting in the presence of a provincial government with a two-thirds majority is unacceptable,” he said.

“The provincial assembly, cabinet and government are fully functional and intact,” the PTI leader asserted, terming Kundi’s act an “attack on the Constitution and democracy”.

Afridi contended that the purpose of the governor’s “unconstitutional activities” was to “provoke the provincial government and force it to react”.

However, he advised PTI workers to stay peaceful and abide by the law and the Constitution.

Calling on the province’s chief secretary and IG, the chief minister urged them not to comply with any unconstitutional or illegal order from anyone if he does not order them to do so.

He reiterated that KP’s people and administration had made “countless sacrifices” in the fight against terrorism.

“If someone pushes you to follow any unconstitutional order, do not follow it. It can damage our province or the country.”

He also called on the chief secretary to urge the provincial administration not to indulge in any unconstitutional activity and to take action against those who were accused of corrupt practices.

The chief minister then took aim at Kundi’s PPP, blaming ex-president Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, along with General Yahya Khan, for the separation of East Pakistan, now Bangladesh.

He accused President Asif Ali Zardari of “intending to make another East Pakistan here“.

“We will not allow any conspiracy to break up Pakistan to succeed,” he asserted.

“The party that raised the slogan of democracy separated Bangladesh from Pakistan in the past for its personal interests,” he alleged.

“Prioritising personal interests over national interests has been the PPP’s practice,” he further claimed.

Responding to Afridi, Kundi said on Geo News’ programme ‘Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Saath’ said he called the meeting in light keeping in view the prevalent terrorism in the province.

He then went on accusing the PTI of facilitating and supporting terrorism.

The remarks by the CM and the governor come amid heightened tensions between the Centre and the PTI-led opposition, with the latter going ahead with its long march despite warnings from the Centre of action against any such move.

Hours-long talks over the weekend between a joint delegation of the government and PPP, and the opposition alliance ended in a deadlock, with both sides blaming the other for the breakdown.

Political temperatures have also remained high due to speculations of the Centre imposing governor’s rule in the province, with Kundi and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi discussing the move on Sunday.

‘Policy shift is necessary’

The KP CM also reiterated his objection to the Centre’s counterterrorism policy and defended his government’s efforts in supporting the police in the fight against terrorism.

He contended that terrorism had been “imposed on the province again”, asserting that the PTI-led provincial government had always supported the police and the people of KP.

Afridi maintained that he had been making efforts to strengthen the police, the Counter-Terrorism Department and Special Branch since he took the oath on Oct 15, 2025.

“The KP police have the most modern weapons and equipment compared with any other police force in Pakistan,” the chief minister said.

He contended that the federal government had always treated KP like a “stepchild”.

“The tribal districts were merged into KP in 2018, but they have not been fully integrated financially to this day,” CM Afridi claimed, adding that the financial rights of the tribal districts agreed upon at the time of their merger had not been provided yet.

The PTI leader went on to claim that federal governments had “continuously imposed military operations” on KP since 2004.

“People displaced by the federal government’s wrong policies kept crying on the streets, but they have still not received full compensation,” he said, adding that nearly Rs100 billion in compensation were still outstanding.

“Those whose homes were destroyed, families affected and mosques demolished are still wandering from pillar to post for their compensation.”

He highlighted that while a compensation of only Rs400,000 per household had been fixed for tribal families, they had not even been paid the promised amount.

Afridi stressed that a commitment was also made to provide between Rs370million and Rs380m per month to displaced people from North Waziristan at the Baka Khel camp. “The displaced people of Baka Khel are still not being provided the monthly amount as promised.”

“It is the provincial government’s responsibility to stand with people displaced by the federal government’s wrong policies,” the chief minister stated, adding that his government had provided Rs21bn for displaced people.

“The provincial government also has to bear responsibility for losses caused by military operations and collateral damage as a result of drone attacks,” Afridi said.

He also remarked that the individuals making decisions in the federal government had no sense of the difficulties faced by the people as a result of those decisions.

“If the federal government is sincere with KP, it should upgrade the province’s NFC (National Finance Commission) share and pay its outstanding dues of around Rs125bn to the province that has sacrificed 80,000 precious lives,” he demanded.

Afridi reaffirmed that KP had to fight terrorism as well as deal with the situation created by the federal government’s policies.

“The KP government and police are serious about maintaining law and order. Turning the police into personal servants and assigning them other tasks is wrong,” he declared.

“If the policy of KP’s stakeholders is followed, peace can be established within 100 days,” the PTI leader insisted.

He questioned why peace could not be established in the province “despite 14,000 intelligence-based operations and 22 major military operations over 22 years”, terming it a “failure of the federal policy”.

Afridi maintained that if the issue of peace still exists in KP even after 22 years, the federal government should change its policy against terrorism if it was “serious in doing so”.

“The excuse that KP is not cooperating is unacceptable; the same policy is also failing in Balochistan,” he claimed, as both provinces have witnessed an increase in terrorist activities in recent years.

“The Balochistan government is cooperating with the federal government, but peace has still not been established there,” Afridi said, claiming the Centre’s counterterrorism policy was neither effective in KP nor in Balochistan.

“A shift in policy is necessary. KP can establish peace within 100 days,” he reaffirmed.

In his address, Afridi also once again criticised Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz’s remarks that her province faced no threats from India, despite the state’s narrative of the presence of Indian proxies in Pakistan in the face of Fitna al Hindustan.

Asif says ‘enough is enough’

Meanwhile, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif assailed the PTI-led KP government for continuing its “complete detachment from terrorism in the province and criminal indifference”.

“Enough is enough!!!” he wrote in a post on X.

“The PTI provincial government is roaming the streets for a so-called failed political long march, while its facilitators have unleashed a fresh wave of terrorism against the people of KP during this very time,” he said.

The minister recalled Tuesday’s attacks in Dera Ismail Khan, where customs officials were among five people killed.

He remarked that the entire provincial cabinet, including the chief minister, was “numb to this serious matter and fully engrossed in their politically failed long march”.

“As always, these insensitive and shameless people did not even condemn the innocent murder of these five individuals in DI Khan, offered no condolences to the grieving families, did not attend their funerals or, at the very least, visit their homes to express regret,” Asif regretted.

“This is inexcusable by any standard.”

Instead, the defence minister noted, the KP CM had scheduled a meeting today at his party’s behest to reprimand the IG and chief secretary for attending the governor’s security meeting.

“The chief minister and his cabinet of a province under the scourge of terrorism have completely abandoned the province’s people to the mercy of the terrorists. That is why the people of KP are protesting against the provincial government on the streets in various areas.

“This can no longer be tolerated,” Asif declared.

The defence minister accused the KP government of being in “complete collusion” with terrorists, saying there was evidence available of “its facilitator ecosystem, which every Pakistani has witnessed with their own eyes over the past three years”.

Recalling past arrests of ex-premier Nawaz Sharif and his family members, as well as PML-N leaders, Asif asserted: “Time has proven that the allegations were just allegations and they were imprisoned on Imran Khan’s behest.”

Yet, he stressed, the PML-N fulfilled its parliamentary role responsibly under the Constitution and did not hold the country and institutions “hostage”.

“It fought a legal and constitutional battle in the courts and parliament. It did not ally with the Taliban,” Asif declared.

The defence minister said that the “time has come to make crucial decisions”.

“KP cannot be left any longer to the mercy of incompetent, insensitive rulers and Taliban allies,” he avowed.

Asif further stressed that the unity of the country cannot be put at risk. “An entire province cannot be held hostage. Enough is enough.”

item.title: Australia prepare for first test in South Africa since'Sandpapergate'
item.description:
Australia play their first test in South Africa since the 2018 ball-tampering scandal when they start a three-match series in Durban on Friday, with the visitors unlikely to face more than a few heckles over the incident that rocked the sport eight years ago.

The tourists efforts to roughen up the ball using sandpaper, and aid reverse swing, in Cape Town in March 2018 were caught on camera and led to a major reckoning for the game in Australia, with captain Steve Smith among those banned for their role in the subterfuge.

South Africa have played tests in Australia since Sandpapergate, and Australia have toured South Africa in the interim for limited-overs internationals.

The scandal has attracted little media focus in South Africa over recent weeks in comparison to the attention devoted to the incident in the Australian press.

After dethroning Australia last year in a thrilling World Test Championship final at Lords to win a first major title, South Africa are focused on improving their chances of a return to the final at the end of the 202527 WTC cycle.

Australia are also in need of a boost after a surprise home test defeat by Bangladesh in August and with an Ashes tour to England starting next June.

The pitch at Kingsmead often proves a fickle track but should offer the spinners a chance to play a leading role in a change from South Africas usually seamer-friendly surfaces.

It is unusual for South Africas chances to be largely entrusted to their spin attack, but Simon Harmer and Keshav Maharaj wreaked havoc in India last November when they triumphed in their last two test outings.

Spin was also a key factor for the home side as they beat Australia in the recent One-Day International series.

South Africa may therefore opt to rest frontline attack bowler Kagiso Rabada from the test as he continues his comeback from a hamstring injury.

Injury to Australia all-rounder Cameron Green opens up a chance at number five for Cooper Connolly, or a fairytale return for 34-year-old Nic Maddinson after recovering from cancer.

South Africas also has a choice to make over their number three batsman, with coach Shukri Conrad having several options including a potential first cap for 30-year-old Marques Ackerman.

item.title: Yemen’s Houthis say struck Riyadh airport, other Saudi sites
item.description:
SAUDI-YEMEN-IRAN-US-ISRAEL-WAR

Iran-backed Houthis said Monday they had struck Riyadh’s international airport, an oil refinery and other sites in Saudi Arabia, as the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said they had destroyed Houthi targets on the Red Sea coast.

Pakistan and Turkey have pledged to deploy troops to Saudi Arabia under a new mutual defence pact following weeks of Houthi attacks, as Riyadh and its Yemeni government allies began an ambitious push aimed at retaking all territory held by the group.

The fighting in Yemen has become the most active front in the Middle East war in recent weeks, displacing more than 184,000 people, the United Nations says, and deepening the conflict that has engulfed the wider region.

The Houthis previously controlled much of northern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa and the western city of Hodeida, but seized swathes of coastline last month along the Red Sea and key Bab al-Mandab Strait, in Yemen’s deadliest fighting in years.

The Houthis have also been attacking neighbouring Saudi Arabia since Yemen’s civil war flared back to life and have declared a maritime blockade on its ships.

The Yemeni military said it carried out more than 1,000 strikes and began an offensive against Sanaa, while the Saudi-led coalition supporting the internationally recognised government said 100 warplanes flew sorties at dawn.

Turki Al-Malki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, said on X that its naval forces had hit “military targets” belonging to the Houthis in Hodeida on the Red Sea coast.

They “destroyed weapons depots, facilities storing booby-trapped boats and naval mines” and had “thwarted a planned attack” targeting waterways in the southern Red Sea, he said.

Later, the military said it had driven the Houthis from the area surrounding the Bab al-Mandeb Strait—a vital route for maritime traffic—including the port city of Mocha, Dhubab airport and Al-Omari military camp.

They also said they expelled the Houthis from several areas in Taiz in the southwest, where deadly fighting has surged in recent days.

Military sources stopped short of confirming an official announcement of Mocha’s recapture, saying that pro-government forces had cut off the only supply route to the port.

UN ‘deeply concerned’

Loud explosions rattled the Saudi capital on Monday evening, with a Houthi spokesman saying the group had hit King Khalid International Airport, a refinery belonging to state oil giant Aramco and other targets in the kingdom’s south.

It came a day after Yemen’s government announced the lofty goal of retaking all Houthi territory—home to most of the country’s population, and much of it held for more than a decade.

Representatives of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey held an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday under the auspices of a joint defence agreement signed in August committing them to come to each other’s aid in the event of any attack.

They also agreed “to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom”.

The statement did not specify what role the troops would fill once in Saudi Arabia.

A spokesman for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting”, and condemned “the continued Houthi cross-border attacks” on Saudi Arabia.

Houthi attacks have repeatedly targeted Saudi oil infrastructure, as well as its tankers in the Red Sea.

A source in the Saudi energy sector told AFP that an attack Sunday had again halted pumping by the East-West pipeline to the Red Sea, a key conduit for the kingdom’s exports since Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the wider Middle East war.

Crude prices had already been soaring as a result of the Middle East war before the Houthis began targeting the world’s largest oil exporter.

Saudi Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser warned on Monday that global oil stockpiles were “scarily thin” owing to the war.

“The system is already straining,” Nasser told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London.

item.title: Bangladesh to buy 10 aircraft from Airbus, deal tomorrow
item.description:
After Boeing, the government is now set to purchase 10 aircraft from European aircraft manufacturer Airbus. A deal between state-owned Biman Bangladesh Airlines and Airbus will be signed tomorrow, Wednesday.

According to a statement issued by Biman Bangladesh Airlines, the signing ceremony, titled 'Spreading Our Wings Together,' will be held at a hotel in the capital. Neither Bangladesh nor Airbus has yet disclosed how much the 10 aircraft will cost.

Under the proposed agreement, Biman will purchase four A350-900s and six A321neos from Airbus. The wide-body A350-900s will primarily be used on long-haul international routes, while the narrow-body A321neos will be deployed on regional and medium-haul routes.

The Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism said Airbus could begin delivering the aircraft in 2033. The aircraft could be added to Biman’s fleet in phases through 2036 or 2037.

25 more aircraft to come from Boeing

Before signing the deal with Airbus, Biman signed two separate agreements this year to purchase a total of 25 aircraft from US aircraft manufacturer Boeing.

In the first deal, signed on 30 April, Biman agreed to purchase 14 aircraft for about USD 3.7 billion (approximately Tk 454 billion). The order includes eight 787-10 Dreamliners, two 787-9s and four 737-8s.

In the second deal, signed in New York on 23 September on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, Biman agreed to purchase another 11 aircraft. These include five 787-10s and six 737-8 MAX aircraft.

The Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism said deliveries of the Boeing aircraft could begin in 2031. It will take 11 to 12 years to receive all the aircraft.

The ministry said Biman will not have to make payments immediately after the agreements are signed. Payment will be made when each aircraft is delivered. However, Biman authorities have requested that at least one aircraft be delivered in 2027 or 2028.

Biman’s current fleet

Biman currently has 19 aircraft in its fleet, including 14 Boeing aircraft and five Dash 8s.

However, two aircraft in the fleet are close to becoming unserviceable. The remaining 17 are also expected to be phased out within the next few years. To meet immediate demand, Biman is therefore trying to lease 10 more aircraft. Despite several attempts, the state-owned airline has yet to lease any aircraft.

Once Airbus’ 10 aircraft and the 25 Boeing aircraft under contract are added, Biman will have 35 new aircraft in the coming years. Including its current 19 aircraft, the airline’s fleet will exceed 50 aircraft.

According to Biman, of the 35 new aircraft, 19 will be wide-body aircraft and 16 will be narrow-body aircraft.

Most of Biman’s current fleet is made up of aircraft manufactured by US-based Boeing. With the addition of Airbus aircraft, Biman Bangladesh Airlines will, for the first time, operate a fleet comprising aircraft from both US and European manufacturers.
